Somerset

UA · England · E06000066 · 69 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 126% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Somerset's year-end treasury report shows borrowing of £716m against a £990m ceiling, with everything compliant — but 39.4% of the debt falls due within twelve months, close to the council's own 50% limit, so a large slice must be refinanced at whatever rates arrive. Housing-account financing costs took 11% of housing income this year and the council's own projections take that to 18.3% by 2030/31. The legacy commercial property portfolio (bought for £301m, written down heavily) is being sold off: £33.3m of sales this year at a £4.7m net gain, £82.3m still to go. watch items

Portsmouth

UA · England · E06000044 · 17 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 315% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Portsmouth ended the year with gross debt of £718m (including £56m of PFI) against investments of £230m — net debt £488m — and took no new borrowing at all, running £292m of internal borrowing instead while new money costs over 5%. Its borrowing need (CFR) is £1,010m, so £292m of real borrowing is deferred, not avoided; the council itself notes this needs ongoing monitoring as the need grows. Net treasury costs came in £0.01m under budget. watch items

Borrowing 208% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Northumberland's borrowing need rose £42.7m to £1,192m and external borrowing rose £64.3m to £895m — the council is steadily converting internal borrowing (down £20.7m to £206m) into real loans. Medway

UA · England · E06000035 · 21 documents (3 read)
Borrowing 243% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Cabinet re-presentation (4 August 2026) of the 2025/26 treasury outturn already seen by the Audit Committee on 24 June, now with the committee's minutes attached — and the minutes add material a lender should read. Borrowing rose £129.5m in one year to £713.5m, driven by capital spending, the need for exceptional financial support and continued lending into Medway Development Company, and the council is now £63m over-borrowed against its £650.5m borrowing CFR. Liquid treasury investments halved to £27m, the interest and financing budget overshot by £5.9m — partly because a budget-build error omitted some borrowing — and officers told members that Grant Thornton has had an MDC cashflow analysis for months without reaching a conclusion on the company's resilience. £20m of LOBO loans carry lender call options exercisable within 12 months. EFS / distress

What the papers say

2025/26 borrowing growth of £129.5m (to £713.5m) attributed to capital spending, "the need for exceptional financial support" and Medway Development Company investment; minutes confirm net borrowing rose £118m with EFS a named driver
The council is funding an EFS-supported revenue position with debt, so its budget balance depends on continued government permission and on the cost of that borrowing. source →
efs-continuing
Exceptional financial support named as a driver of £129.5m borrowing growth
The budget is being propped up by converting losses into debt while the debt pile compounds. source →
efs-continuing
External borrowing £713.5m at 31 March 2026, up £129.5m in the year and £63.0m ABOVE the £650.5m borrowing CFR — the Audit Committee was told borrowing rose above the CFR partly to pre-fund monies owed to the council
Borrowing beyond the underlying need means extra carrying cost and exposes the council to rate risk on cash it is waiting to recover. source →
borrowing-increase
Interest and Financing outturn £23.960m against an £18.107m budget — a £5.853m deficit, with interest paid £28.591m vs £22.381m budgeted after an error in the budget build omitted some borrowing
A structural under-budgeting of debt costs that recurs into 2026/27 eats directly into revenue headroom. source →
debt-servicing-rising
£20m of LOBO loans have call dates within the next 12 months; officers estimate ~£60,000 extra cost if the most likely loan is called and ~£130,000 if all four (coupons 3.6%–4.75%) are called; a £10m Dexia LOBO was already repaid 26/09/25
Calls would crystallise refinancing at today's higher rates on top of an already overspent financing budget. source →
lobo-call-window
£153.4m of loans to subsidiaries (long-term capital debtors £152.1m at 5.91%, up £36.6m in year, mainly Medway Development Company); Grant Thornton has been given an MDC cashflow analysis but "no conclusion had yet been reached" on its financial resilience
A fifth of the council's debt is on-lent to a company whose resilience the external auditor has not yet been able to sign off. source →
company-exposure
Liquid treasury investments fell £25.2m in the year to £26.977m at 31 March 2026 (bank £0.1m, MMF £9.5m, property funds £17.4m) against £713.5m of borrowing
Under 4% investment cover against the debt book leaves little cash buffer if short-term rollover or LOBO calls arrive together. source →
low-liquidity
£215.5m of £687.5m total borrowing is short-term at 30 June 2026 (£90.5m from other local authorities, WAM 0.39 years), plus £47m of HRA loans maturing before the PWLB HRA discount ends in March 2027
Roughly a third of the debt book must be rolled or refinanced within a year in a market the report itself calls volatile. source →
refinancing-risk
£40m of the £50.5m LOBO portfolio has lender call dates within the next 12 months (up from £20m reported for 2025/26); policy is to repay rather than accept a higher rate, funded from cash or new LA/PWLB borrowing
Calls would convert cheap 4.17%-coupon debt into new borrowing at today's rates precisely when liquid cash is thin. source →
lobo-call-window
Liquid treasury investments of £36.4m (long-term £14.3m, short-term £19.1m, cash £3.0m) against £687.5m of borrowing at 30 June 2026
About 5% investment cover leaves the repay-LOBOs-from-cash plan and daily cashflow dependent on continuous access to the inter-authority market. source →
low-liquidity

York

UA · England · E06000014 · 54 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 244% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

York runs lean: gross debt of £400.4m against treasury investments of just £4.4m — essentially no cash cushion, with the capital programme funded by using every pound of internal cash before borrowing. The forward path is the story: the borrowing need rises from £514.8m to £638.0m by 2029/30 (the General Fund element alone from £332m to £449m) as capital spending steps up from £86.7m this year to a planned £153.7m peak in 2027/28 — a steady multi-year pipeline of new borrowing demand. watch items

Rother

NMD · England · E07000064 · 11 documents (0 read)
Borrowing 170% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Rother's 2023/24 treasury outturn shows cash running down fast: investments halved from £29.8m at Q3 to £14.5m at 31 March 2024 as the council paused borrowing and funded capital spending from its own balances, leaving it £17.9m under-borrowed against a £49.6m capital financing requirement with external debt steady at £31.7m. Interest income of £1.427m beat the £586k budget and the overall treasury surplus was £841k. The watch items are concentration rather than compliance: a £4.6m loan at 9% to its wholly-owned housing company with a further £41.5m of company borrowing/lending programmed for 2024/25, £8m in pooled property funds now worth £922,707 less than cost (shielded by the IFRS9 statutory override until March 2025), and a £32.8m commercial property portfolio. All borrowing stayed comfortably within the £192.8m authorised limit. watch items

Winchester

NMD · England · E07000094 · 9 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 691% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Winchester's 2025/26 treasury outturn is clean and fully compliant: £159.3m of debt, all PWLB and all related to housing (HRA), at an average 3.06% with 17.8 years average maturity, against £16.6m of investments including a £5m pooled property fund protected by the IFRS9 override until April 2029. In-year it took £10m of new PWLB loans and repaid £5.2m, and investment income of £1.4m more than doubled the £0.6m budget. The forward story is a growing borrowing need: the liability benchmark shows the net loans requirement rising from £142.0m to £191.1m by March 2028 while existing loans amortise down to £136.8m — roughly £64m of new borrowing to find within two years if the capital programme is delivered as planned. Only 7% of debt matures within 12 months, well inside the 25% limit. watch items

Dover

NMD · England · E07000108 · 26 documents (3 read)
Borrowing 243% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Dover ended 2025/26 with £46.5m in externally managed strategic pooled bond, multi-asset and property funds (£2.1m income in the year, a 4.57% average return) while running day-to-day cash on £55m of short-term loans borrowed from other councils. That short-term stance cost it: borrowing costs came in £894k above the original £1,091k budget as inter-authority money became scarcer and housing development drew cash. The council breached its own interest-rate-risk indicator — a 1% rate move now shifts net interest by £693k against a £500k target — and has responded by raising the 2026/27 limit to £750k rather than shrinking the exposure. All other treasury and prudential limits were complied with, and no debt rescheduling is considered worthwhile. watch items

Chorley

NMD · England · E07000118 · 22 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 486% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Chorley ended 2025/26 with £83.6m of gross debt (£63.0m PWLB plus £20m of short-term loans from other local authorities) against a £110.6m capital financing requirement and year-end investments of just £11.2m. Debt actually fell £4.0m in the year — no new long-term PWLB was taken and capital spending came in at £10.1m against a £46.8m original estimate — but financing costs still consumed 19.07% of the net revenue stream, 1.38 points above budget and an unusually heavy load for a shire district. The £20m of local-authority loans (about a quarter of the debt book) must be refinanced within the year against thin cash, with the council £27m internally borrowed. All borrowing limits were complied with throughout the year. watch items

South Ribble

NMD · England · E07000126 · 27 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 1% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

South Ribble is effectively debt-free: gross debt at 31 March 2026 was just £42k of finance leases, with the £25.1m capital financing requirement met entirely from the council's own cash and no external borrowing taken in the year. Investments stood at £22.3m at year end (average daily balance £37.1m, earning £1,503k at 3.63%), including £11m of term deposits with Blackpool and Bournemouth, Christchurch & Poole councils, and financing costs are a modest 3.28% of the net revenue stream. The trend to watch is slow cash erosion: average balances fell 16.6% year-on-year and interest earned dropped 33% as capital spending is funded internally, while the CFR rose from £19.7m to £25.1m. All prudential indicators and counterparty limits were complied with. verified quiet

Charnwood

NMD · England · E07000130 · 39 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 338% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Charnwood ran its cash down sharply in 2025/26: treasury investments fell from £37.4m to £16.2m as capital spending — including £5.0m of unfinanced HRA works — was funded internally rather than borrowing at elevated rates, swinging the council from £14.4m net investor to £11.1m net debtor. Debt is £76.2m of legacy HRA PWLB at an average 3.38% after a scheduled £2m repayment, against a £103.5m capital financing requirement, leaving £27.3m internally borrowed. The report states plainly that borrowing long-term 'will be necessary' to fund future unfinanced capital spend and maturing debt, with a Capital Plan update due in autumn 2026 — against 1-year PWLB at 5.04% and 50-year at 6.08% at year end. It also exited both its pooled property funds (Hermes fund merger, Lothbury wind-up), crystallising just over £1m of losses which were fully provided for. watch items

South Kesteven

NMD · England · E07000141 · 27 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 397% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

South Kesteven's debt is all housing (HRA) borrowing and edged down to £76.548m at an average 2.57%, against a capital financing requirement of £102.722m — so £26.174m of the borrowing need is covered by the council's own cash rather than loans. The story is on the cash side: investments fell from £62.767m to £43.141m because the capital programme was paid for wholly from reserves, and the council itself says cashflow management is becoming more challenging as reserve levels continue to decrease. Investment income of £2.718m came in £0.030m under budget after HRA reserves were drawn to meet in-year spending pressures. Internal audit gave the treasury function a substantial assurance opinion, and there were no liquidity difficulties in the year. watch items

Newark and Sherwood

NMD · England · E07000175 · 81 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 510% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

A two-page covering summary of Newark and Sherwood's year-end treasury position ahead of Full Council on 14 July 2026, prepared on draft accounts. Total borrowings fell from £109.799m to £104.923m over 2025/26, putting total external debt (including £6.297m of other long-term liabilities) at £111.220m. Investments fell from £49.028m to £38.140m, of which £12.5m is long-term. The council states there were no breaches of approved prudential indicators; all the detail (CFR, maturity profile, indicator tables) sits in Appendix A, a separate agenda document. verified quiet

Arun

NMD · England · E07000224 · 15 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 115% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Arun ended 2025/26 with £35.46m of PWLB debt — four maturity loans taken in 2012 for HRA housing self-financing at an average 3.40%, the first not repayable until 2030 — against a capital financing requirement of £52.06m, leaving £16.6m covered by internal cash instead of loans. No new borrowing was taken during the year, and planned borrowing-funded capital spending largely did not happen (£2.956m unfinanced capital expenditure against an original £27.913m), so the CFR barely moved. Investment income was £2.3m against a £2.02m budget on average balances of about £53m. The council's two CCLA pooled funds are worth £559k less than the £7m put in — a loss parked behind the IFRS 9 statutory override until March 2029, with a £500k equalisation reserve set aside against it. verified quiet

Chichester

NMD · England · E07000225 · 26 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 0% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Chichester is debt-free — no external borrowing and a nil capital financing requirement right across the forecast to 2029/30 — and held £118.757m of investments at 31 March 2026, up £7.2m in the year. Treasury income of £6.030m beat the £4.164m budget, mainly because the council locked in higher-yielding deposits (including £51m with other local authorities) ahead of rate cuts. Its £36.8m of externally managed pooled funds have produced £12.3m of income since purchase in 2016 against a cumulative £3.2m capital loss, which sits behind the IFRS 9 statutory override until April 2029. The £13.13m directly owned commercial property portfolio produced a £640k net surplus, though voids rose to 5.4% from 2.27% a year earlier. verified quiet

Tameside

MD · England · E08000008 · 32 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 62% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Tameside cut borrowing by £20m to £126.269m in 2025/26 — repaying a £10m short-term loan and buying out a £10m Barclays loan early at a c.£2.8m discount — but its cash fell much faster: investments dropped £40.610m to just £22.030m, all in money market funds, as capital spending was funded from balances to defer borrowing in a high-rate market. Interest earned came in £0.886m under budget at £3.789m because balances fell quicker than forecast. £30m of the remaining debt is LOBO loans with semi-annual call options, and Dexia has exercised its option to raise the rate on a £5m LOBO at the 16 June 2026 call date — the council chose to prepay in full and is weighing refinancing. Tameside is also owed £37.440m by Manchester Airport Group (a £29.632m shareholder loan plus £8.954m of COVID-deferred interest); the airport shareholding itself paid no dividend this year, though car-park dividends and loan interest brought in £4.735m. watch items

Wigan

MD · England · E08000010 · 29 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 120% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Wigan's year-end treasury review shows a compliant but growing debt book: loan debt rose £52.2m to £440.2m in 2025/26 (£67m of new loans at 4.34%-4.74%), against a borrowing need (CFR) of £623.3m, leaving the council £137.2m under-borrowed — running on internal cash rather than external debt. Treasury investments rose to £43.2m earning 5.17%, and all borrowing stayed inside the £678.7m authorised limit. The new borrowing was deliberately short-dated (all four 2025/26 loans mature by June 2027) to avoid locking in long-term rates above 5%, so the council returns to the market to refinance from late 2026 onward. watch items

St. Helens

MD · England · E08000013 · 16 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 66% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

St Helens ran a deliberately under-borrowed book in 2025/26, funding capital spend from its own cash while taking one £25m PWLB loan in April 2025 at 4.59% to lock in a rate — and the report warns more borrowing 'will be required imminently' for capital schemes. Debt stood at £157.5m at 31 March 2026 against a £220.7m borrowing need, with investments of £97.2m (including £15.1m held for Merseyside Recycling and Waste Authority and £10.3m for schools). Net treasury costs came in £2.8m under budget at £1.8m, helped by deferred borrowing and above-benchmark investment returns. £15m of LOBO loans are profiled at their next lender call dates, which makes the maturity ladder look short-term even though contractual maturities exceed 50 years. watch items

Calderdale

MD · England · E08000033 · 13 documents (2 read)
Borrowing 77% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Calderdale ended 2025/26 with just £2.68m of external investments — a single NatWest call account, down from £6.2m a year earlier — against £137.6m of PWLB debt: the cash cushion is essentially gone. The report is unusually candid about why: years of SEND (schools funding) deficits and reserve drawdowns have worsened cashflow, forcing rolling short-term borrowing from other councils (£305k of interest in the year) even as £9.98m of PWLB debt matured without replacement. Treasury costs overran budget by £654k because investment income fell £1.54m short of plan. Internal borrowing will need replacing with new long-term PWLB loans in 2026/27, so a step-up in external debt is coming against a CFR of £237.3m. watch items

Gateshead

MD · England · E08000037 · 52 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 305% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

A broadly quiet year at Gateshead: external debt was near-flat at £670.2m (up £4.3m) against a £764.7m borrowing need excluding PFI, every prudential indicator was met, and treasury delivered £2.45m of net savings against budget. The council remains £94.5m internally borrowed, and investments fell to £34.8m (from £47.1m) held very short — an average duration of 2 days including overnight — while the debt book itself is long-dated, with under 2% of fixed-rate loans maturing within 12 months. The watch item is company lending: a further loan was advanced to the wholly-owned Gateshead Energy Company during the year (after the budget was set), and the council holds Newcastle Airport loan notes which paid deferred interest in 2025/26; neither balance is quantified in this report. watch items

Barnet

LBO · England · E09000003 · 38 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 345% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Barnet's borrowing is scaling fast: having historically funded capital spending from internal cash, the council borrowed a further £159.44m in 2025/26, lifting total debt from £1.157bn to £1.317bn, with another £49.36m of existing debt refinanced in-year. Treasury investments fell to £49.875m (from £61.621m) — described as 'broadly at the council's liquidity buffer', the minimum cash its strategy allows — and the report acknowledges managing 'relatively low cash balances' through a volatile rate environment. Outside the treasury book sit £422.731m of non-treasury investments, including loans to council-owned subsidiaries, third-party developers and community organisations, plus gilts held against Brent Cross Plot 1 commercial agreements. Loan-level detail, the CFR and the maturity ladder are in Appendix A, presented with the outturn to Cabinet on 9 June 2026. watch items

Bexley

LBO · England · E09000004 · 32 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 123% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Bexley ended 2025/26 with £249.6m of debt (£224.6m long-dated PWLB at 3.34% plus £25m of short-term loans from other councils at an average 5.97%) against just £10.1m of investments, after cash balances more than halved in the year from £21.6m. The £25m of temporary borrowing was taken in February-March 2026 purely to keep the council liquid, at rates up to 7%, and all of it falls due in April 2026. The CFR outturn was £318.6m against £249.6m of borrowing, and the CIPFA liability benchmark shows existing loans are insufficient to meet the projected CFR, so more long-term borrowing is coming. All prudential limits were met and no limit was exceeded on any day. watch items

Camden

LBO · England · E09000007 · 15 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 104% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Camden took no new borrowing in 2025/26 and held external debt flat at £294m (£169m PWLB at 4.57%, £124m LOBOs at 4.43%, £1m community bond), but its CFR jumped £50m to £812m, pushing under-borrowing (capital spend financed from its own cash instead of loans) to £518m. The council says this internal borrowing saves about £10.4m a year versus borrowing at current rates, but also that planned use of earmarked reserves will create an external borrowing requirement within 12-24 months, and that investments were drawn down in-year to support cash flow as service demand outpaced funding. Headline investments of £197m flatter the picture: £159m of that is held on behalf of the North London Waste Authority. The report itself flags a greater likelihood that LOBO lenders will exercise their rate-reset options as market rates have risen. A £6.4m loan was made in April 2025 to wholly-owned Camden Living Housing Association; all prudential indicators were met. watch items

Hammersmith and Fulham

LBO · England · E09000013 · 30 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 177% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Hammersmith and Fulham borrowed a further £35m from the PWLB and repaid £16m in 2024/25, lifting debt from £269.2m to £288.3m (all fixed rate, average 3.75%), with 82.4% of the debt serviced by the housing account. The striking move is on the other side of the balance sheet: cash invested fell 72% in the year, from £159.3m to £44.2m, all now held short-term in money market funds and one £10m local-authority deposit. The total CFR rose from £614m to £766.7m, so the council is heavily under-borrowed (HRA internal borrowing alone is £222m) and future capital spend implies substantial further borrowing. All prudential indicators were met, with only 2% of debt maturing within 12 months, and the figures remain subject to external audit. watch items

Haringey

LBO · England · E09000014 · 30 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 402% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Haringey's debt is growing fast: loans rose £232.1m during 2025/26 to £1,213.4m at 31 March 2026, funding a large capital programme the council says will continue to be financed largely by new borrowing in coming years. Cash is managed very tight - investment balances swung between £13.6m and £184.3m over the year, with the portfolio's weighted average maturity just 1 day and a year-end return of 3.75%. The Section 151 officer reports full compliance with the Treasury Management Code except lease levels measured against the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit, an exception first reported at Quarter 3. This is the covering report; the detailed tables (investment position, borrowing detail, indicator-by-indicator compliance) sit in Appendix 1, a separate document. watch items

Westminster

LBO · England · E09000033 · 19 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 254% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Westminster took no new long-term borrowing in 2025/26 and debt edged down to £569m (mostly £386m of 2019-arranged forward loans at an average 2.579%, plus £113.6m PWLB and £40m LOBOs), while cash invested fell £157m to £306.3m as internal borrowing funded the capital programme - the council is £483m under-borrowed against a total closing CFR of £1,748m. Investment income came in £11.8m under budget (£29.7m vs £41.5m), a shortfall that flows straight to the revenue account. The Operational Boundary (£605m) was exceeded, with gross debt at £855m, because the A2Dominion lease transaction from April 2025 added £257m of lease liabilities to the CFR after the strategy was set; the statutory Authorised Limit (£1,641m) was not breached. The council retained its Moody's Aa3 rating and holds loans and equity in its wholly-owned housing companies (Westminster Builds), with amounts detailed in the separate Integrated Investment Framework rather than this report. watch items

Gloucestershire

CTY · England · E10000013 · 24 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 47% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Gloucestershire's borrowing rose £31.1m to £259.5m in 2025/26 (average cost 4.43%), driven by £56.1m of new market borrowing including seven temporary LA-to-LA loans at 4.15%-4.7% taken to manage liquidity; the CFR rose to £497.9m. Investments fell £8m to £193.4m, and the council states plainly that balances and reserves are reducing because of internal borrowing on the capital programme and the increasing SEND deficit - though no deficit figure is given in this report. Nearly half the portfolio (£90m principal, market value £86.6m) sits in long-dated strategic pooled funds protected by a statutory override extended to 31 March 2029; within these, a social housing REIT has fallen to £3.2m from £5m invested, with the valuer citing distressed housing associations in the sector. Three Dexia LOBOs (£22.05m) saw an increased probability of lender calls as rates rose, but none were called. All activity complied with the strategy and prudential indicators. watch items

Lancashire

CTY · England · E10000017 · 10 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 107% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Lancashire ended 2025/26 with £948.8m of borrowing (down £98.8m, with maturing debt partly replaced by internal borrowing) and £531.7m of investments, but around 60% of its debt now matures within 12 months — nearly double its own one-third aim — after it deliberately stayed short while long-term rates spiked following the war in Iran. Rather than pay roughly £1.2m extra to extend the debt, it is asking Full Council to raise the under-12-month maturity limit from 50% to 75%, cut all lower maturity limits to 0%, and adopt a departure from the CIPFA Code's maturity measurement convention. The treasury budget overspent by £2.7m in-year (investment returns below budget plus extra working-capital borrowing to finance the schools-grant deficit), covered from an earmarked reserve, and its Very Long-Term Investment Portfolio remains worth significantly less than was paid for it, with no figures disclosed in this report. watch items

Leicestershire

CTY · England · E10000018 · 42 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 30% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Leicestershire's debt keeps shrinking: it repaid £44.5m of PWLB loans in 2025/26 — including £15.3m of 6.25-7.88% loans bought back at a £3.5m premium in March 2026 — taking external debt to £130.5m, its lowest for over 20 years, against a £387.5m investment portfolio and £388m of cash. The one indicator breach is a direct result: capital financing costs as a share of net revenue exceeded target because of those premiums, which the council expects to save nearly £1m a year in future interest. What remains of the debt book is dominated by £93.5m of market loans whose lenders can propose rate rises at pre-set dates (LOBO-type), a live consideration with gilt yields at their highest this century. The council has not raised a new external loan since August 2010, is £63m under-borrowed, and earned £16.6m treasury interest against a £12m budget. watch items

Worcestershire

CTY · England · E10000034 · 47 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 137% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Worcestershire's borrowing jumped £118.1m in 2025/26 to £725.2m — including £221.2m of new PWLB — as internal borrowing collapsed from £123.9m to £27.7m and was replaced with external debt, and short-term borrowing more than doubled to £225.2m, deliberately breaching the council's own 25% under-one-year maturity limit (31.1% actual) rather than lock in long-term rates it hopes will fall. Year-end liquidity is thin: net cash and investments of £16.3m against the £725.2m debt pile, with the bank account £27.6m overdrawn at 31 March (gross money-market and bond fund holdings were £52.7m, including fire authority monies, 99% accessible within 28 days). The report also discloses a £180.8m negative DSG schools reserve 'impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet', and the council rates the current treasury risk HIGH (residual medium). Net treasury costs still came in £6.4m under budget at £31.8m. watch items

Torfaen

WPA · Wales · W06000020 · 11 documents (1 read)
MHCLG: England only rank vs peers →

Torfaen's treasury year was quiet and compliant: external debt fell £8.2m to £123.4m (all fixed rate, average 4.20%), financing costs are just 3.54% of net revenue, and borrowing sits within its £129.1m capital financing requirement and £150.7m authorised limit. The council took no new long-term borrowing while rates were high, instead rolling temporary loans from other councils — £30m outstanding at year end with an average remaining life of about a month at 5.34% — a deliberate wait-for-rates-to-fall stance it says it will unwind when there is a financial case. The only indicator exceeded was investment interest-rate exposure (£187,000 sensitivity vs £150,000 assumed), which worked in the council's favour, and investments of £16.5m stayed above the £10m MIFID II floor throughout. watch items

West Berkshire

UA · England · E06000037 · 19 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 182% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Covering report for West Berkshire's Annual Governance Statement, which will sit inside the 2025/26 financial statements audited by KPMG. The council states plainly that its financial position "remains extremely difficult" with an in-year overspend, being managed through a Finance Improvement Plan, and financial resilience heads the list of governance issues for a second year. The most concrete lender-relevant item is the schools funding deficit: the High Needs (DSG) deficit has been growing and stays off the general fund balance sheet only via the statutory override, which the report says runs to 31 March 2028, and the council's headline action for 2026/27 is securing High Needs Stability Grant funding to write off circa 90% of that deficit. No deficit figure is given in this paper — it is quantified in the Final Local Government Finance Settlement 2026/27 and the accompanying DfE/MHCLG technical notes. Local government reorganisation, if the submitted proposals including West Berkshire are accepted, is flagged as a further material change ahead. watch items

Isle of Wight

UA · England · E06000046 · 34 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 124% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

EY's Auditor's Annual Report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carries three messages a lender should weigh together. First, the accounts are dark: EY disclaimed its opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements — the third consecutive disclaimed year after 2022/23 and 2023/24 under the national audit reset — so there is no audited view of the balance sheet, no going-concern conclusion, and recovery is running a year behind the NAO's rebuild timetable. Second, day-to-day finances are managed but tightening: 2024/25 closed £3.6m underspent only after releasing corporate contingency against social-care overspends, the 2025/26 Q1 forecast is £3.4m over, reserves sit barely above the £8m minimum, and the council has applied for £12.9m of Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 (agreed in principle). Third, EY reported an actual significant weakness in governance arrangements: an independent review published in November 2025 found member conduct breaches, an ineffective standards process and dysfunction, and MHCLG has raised the prospect of a best value notice or inspection. Financial sustainability and value-for-money arrangements were otherwise judged adequate. EFS / distress

Cheshire East

UA · England · E06000049 · 31 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 104% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Covering report presenting the draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025/26 (the AGS itself is Appendix 1, a separate document). Two points matter for a lender. First, the draft AGS has been published alongside the council's draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, with the final versions due by the 31 January 2027 statutory deadline after a further update in October 2026 — the reporting cycle is on its statutory track. Second, the council says no NEW significant governance issues have arisen since the final 2024/25 AGS was approved in February 2026, but the existing ones continue: the draft focuses on updating progress on financial sustainability, improvement and transformation, governance and internal control, leadership capacity, children's services improvement and partnership working. In short, a council still working through a known list of significant issues, with no fresh deterioration disclosed and no figures in this paper. watch items

Westmorland and Furness

UA · England · E06000064 · 56 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 73% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Westmorland and Furness closed 2025/26 with a quiet treasury position: no new external borrowing was taken, the council instead covering previously approved borrowing need from short-term cash reserves rather than paying for new loans. Debt stood at £173.6m (average rate 3.7%) against £74.6m of temporary investments (average 4.07%) at 31 March 2026, and treasury management came in £6.3m under its £14.65m budget thanks to high interest earned on retained cash balances. The report confirms all treasury activity complied with the prudential indicators and the February 2025 strategy. Full Council was also asked to approve a revised 2025-2031 capital programme of £591.1m at outturn, up from £432.1m when first set in February 2025, with outturn slippage of £10.1m and accelerated spend of £12.6m. verified quiet

Rushmoor

NMD · England · E07000092 · 18 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 914% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Rushmoor's unaudited 2025/26 accounts show £149m of borrowing — half of it maturing within 12 months, including £62m of short-term PWLB — against £28.7m of usable reserves, while the £110.6m commercial investment-property estate is written down further and £21.9m of assets sit in held-for-sale. The revenue outturn beat budget (only £2.4m of a budgeted £3.4m reserves drawdown was needed against an approved £5.2m budget gap), but the AGS discloses that external auditor EY has again raised concerns about the council's progress on financial sustainability and resolving its deficit, and is explicitly keeping a public interest report under consideration — on top of disclaimed audit opinions for every year from 2020/21 to 2023/24. Rushmoor is abolished into a new North Hampshire unitary from 1 April 2028 under local government reorganisation. For a lender the direction of travel is mixed: debt fell £17m in the year and the accounting deficit narrowed from £37.0m to £6.0m, but the balance sheet has not been independently verified for years and the auditor's sustainability warning is live. watch items

Thanet

NMD · England · E07000114 · 24 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 144% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Thanet's borrowing is scaling up fast to fund a £189.6m revised 2026/27 capital programme: gross debt stood at £90.5m at 30 June 2026, up from £37.1m a year earlier, and the council's underlying need to borrow (the Capital Financing Requirement) is forecast to nearly double from £92.2m at March 2026 to £180.4m by March 2027 — close under the £191m authorised borrowing limit. A £10m ten-year PWLB loan was drawn in May 2026 at the 4.95% HRA concessionary rate for council-housing capital works. Investments were £44.4m (of which £40.2m in money market funds, all maturities under one year) yielding 3.90% against a 3.75% SONIA benchmark, and the s151 officer reports no limit breaches in the quarter and no difficulties envisaged in complying with the prudential indicators. watch items

A pre-audit covering report asking the committee to approve Wyre's 2025/26 Statement of Accounts; the draft was certified by the s151 officer and published by the 30 June 2026 statutory deadline. The report itself carries no figures — the accounts, capital financing report, revenue variances and the reserves and balances statements all sit in appendices published separately, with the outturn to be folded into the Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2030/31. Blaby

NMD · England · E07000129 · 32 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 26% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Blaby's unaudited 2025/26 accounts show a financially healthy district: the year ended £1.6m better than budget (a £1,613,572 surplus where the Q3 forecast was a £240,689 drawdown from balances), lifting the general fund balance to £8.262m — 43.0% of the 2026/27 net budget requirement, just under the council's own 45% ceiling — with earmarked reserves up £4.0m to £15.6m. Debt is minimal and falling: £4.0m of PWLB loans at 2.08% against a £21.6m capital financing requirement, the £17.6m gap run as internal borrowing (using own cash instead of loans), alongside £19.6m of short-term investments. Behind the good headline sit three watch items: the business-rates collection fund swung from a £2.3m surplus to a £2.7m deficit (Blaby's £1.1m share lands in the 2027/28 budget, and the national business-rates reset 'heavily reduces' retained rates from 2026/27); a residual £0.745m sits in the UBS Triton property fund pending recovery from the terminated Lothbury fund; and a prior-year IFRS 16 leasing error (liabilities understated) was corrected while the pension liability rose from £7.3m to £11.6m. watch items

Melton

NMD · England · E07000133 · 57 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 356% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

A procedural covering report presenting Melton's draft Annual Governance Statement (AGS) for 2025/26 — the yearly self-assessment of internal control that must be published alongside the financial statements. The annual review's overall conclusion is that the council 'continues to have effective arrangements in place to protect the Council's interests and promote good governance'. The AGS itself, including its closing list of areas for improvement, sits in Appendix A (not part of this paper) and will be reviewed by the external auditor alongside the draft statement of accounts before formal sign-off by the Chief Executive and Leader. Nothing in the covering report raises financial-stress, audit-timetable or governance red flags. verified quiet

Broadland

NMD · England · E07000144 · 26 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 0% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Broadland's Annual Governance Statement review for 2025/26, produced in a revised format under the CIPFA/SOLACE Framework Addendum that now requires an explicit conclusion on whether governance is 'fit for purpose'. The review concludes the council's arrangements are fit for purpose with no significant governance issues — only minor control weaknesses, which are listed in section 6 of the AGS itself (an appendix not included in this paper). The 2025/26 internal audit opinion on governance, risk management and control was still being finalised and was to be confirmed at the 30 July meeting. The paper comes from the officer team Broadland shares with South Norfolk but is addressed to Broadland's own Audit Committee; nothing in it signals financial stress. verified quiet

Rotherham

MD · England · E08000018 · 41 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 260% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Quarter 1 monitoring for 2026/27 shows Rotherham running a deliberately under-borrowed, short-term book: £50m of temporary local-authority borrowing was refinanced as it matured (new loans from Greater Manchester CA, East Midlands CCA, West Yorkshire CA and Oxfordshire CC at 4.50–5.00%, replacing loans at 4.15–4.65%), and further short-term borrowing is expected before year-end in anticipation of lower rates — long-term PWLB hit multi-year highs of 6.35% for 50-year money in the quarter. At 30 June 2026 gross external debt was £845.6m against a £1,042.6m operational boundary, £137m (19.3%) of borrowing matures within 12 months, and investments were just £47.7m, all in overnight money market funds, under a stated policy of carrying minimal cash. All treasury and prudential indicators were complied with in the quarter, though the HRA financing-costs ratio (13.89%) is running slightly above its original 13.47% estimate. watch items

Sandwell

MD · England · E08000028 · 41 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 143% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Cover report for Sandwell's draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, published on the council website on 30 June 2026 in line with the statutory deadline; Grant Thornton began fieldwork on 13 July 2026, targeting audit completion by 10 November and final publication by 30 November 2026, well inside the 31 January 2027 backstop. The draft CIES reports net income of £109.6m, with General Fund balances up £10.6m, HRA balances down £1.1m and capital-programme reserves up £15.8m — a strengthening usable-reserves position. One open item: a specialist adviser is reviewing all four PFI financial models for consistency and compliance, and the council cannot yet quantify what adjustments that review will feed into the final accounts. Group accounts consolidate the wholly-owned Sandwell Children's Trust. watch items

Wakefield

MD · England · E08000036 · 31 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 108% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Wakefield's 2025/26 treasury outturn was fully compliant: the CFR rose £13.5m to £571.3m while external borrowing actually fell £3.1m to £377.9m (PWLB £346.4m, other local authorities £26.5m, banks £5m), leaving the council £131.9m under-borrowed and running on internal cash — capital slippage saved £4.2m of borrowing costs and the treasury budget underspent £3.85m. The average rate paid on external debt was 4.80%, and the council flags that the LA-to-LA borrowing market is 'becoming tight' as other authorities chase the same borrow-short-until-rates-fall strategy; investments stood at £57m (£40m in the DMO deposit facility, £17m lent to other councils). A legacy MRP overpayment that has been suppressing the revenue charge for debt is nearly exhausted — £5.3m left, fully used by end-2026/27, after which all MRP hits the revenue budget. Financing costs ran at 11.30% of net revenue (9.68% excluding PFI) against budgets of 13.16% and 9.70%. watch items

Islington ended 2025/26 with £443.6m of borrowing (almost all PWLB at 4.40% average) after taking £57m of new PWLB loans, against a borrowing CFR of £868.5m — an internal-borrowing position of £425m that the report itself says presents a refinancing risk if rates rise significantly. The liability benchmark shows the net loans requirement doubling from £351.6m to about £704m by March 2027 as the housing-led capital programme lands, implying substantial new borrowing in a 5-6% PWLB market. Investments of £92m earned £5.1m against a £1.75m budget, and £33m of that is lent to other local authorities. All prudential indicators were complied with; no LOBOs and no short-term borrowing outstanding at year end. watch items

Derbyshire

CTY · England · E10000007 · 43 documents (1 read)
MHCLG return incomplete rank vs peers →

Derbyshire held borrowing flat at £400.9m in 2025/26 but the mix leans on short money: £124.5m is short-term borrowing from other local authorities (average maturity 0.2 years) and 33% of all debt matures within 12 months, in a market where year-end inter-authority rates spiked to 5-7%. Internal borrowing rose £69m to £302.8m as usable reserves fall — partly because reserves are being used to fund the DSG schools deficit — and the forecast balance sheet assumes an £84m SEN refund from government in 2026-27. Investment income strongly overachieved (£10.9m vs £3.9m budget) and the £11.4m Buxton Crescent Hotel loan was repaid in full when the hotel was sold in December 2025. The £50m nominal strategic pooled funds still carry a stated £4.455m unrealised loss behind the statutory override (extended to April 2029), with a £3.9m reserve held against it; all prudential indicators were complied with. watch items

Powys

WPA · Wales · W06000023 · 24 documents (1 read)
MHCLG: England only rank vs peers →

Powys's Q4 report to 31 March 2026 shows total borrowing down £5.61m over the year to £362.03m even after £25m of new PWLB in Q4, with the CFR closing at £453.34m — £22.7m below the original estimate because capital schemes were reprofiled and extra Welsh Government grants landed. Financing costs came in at 3.8% of net revenue against 4.0% planned, but the report is explicit that the deferred borrowing 'will still be required in the future': the CFR is forecast to reach £614.20m by March 2028. The council was an active short-term lender to other authorities (£35.32m across six loans in Q4, all repaid by March 2026). Aged sundry debt rose £3.0m in the quarter to £15.51m, 73% of the over-three-month debt being hard-to-collect social care charges; all treasury prudential indicators were complied with. watch items

Thurrock

UA · England · E06000034 · 39 documents (0 read)
Borrowing 575% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Thurrock's borrowing need (its capital financing requirement) is around £1.1 billion and edging up over the next three years, of which £371m is the special government permission that lets it treat past losses as capital (the capitalisation direction). External debt of about £846m is expected to grow to roughly £1 billion, and the council itself flags that much of its PWLB borrowing is short-dated, so it must be refinanced often. No change to its debt-repayment (MRP) policy this year. EFS / distress

City of Edinburgh

SCO · Scotland · S12000036 · 46 documents (1 read)
MHCLG: England only rank vs peers →

Edinburgh proposes £581m of additional borrowing over the ten-year capital programme, plus £108m supported by the visitor levy and £38m by place-based growth funding. Crucially, the room for this borrowing is created by changing the policy on how quickly past borrowing is repaid (the loans fund repayment policy — Scotland's equivalent of an MRP change): stretching repayments lowers today's costs but keeps debt outstanding for longer. The change needs full-council ratification. watch items

Croydon

LBO · England · E09000008 · 35 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 388% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Croydon's year-end treasury report shows total borrowing need (CFR) reaching £1,968m — up £133m in a year — of which £108.7m was new capitalisation-direction spending, the borrowing permission that funds day-to-day losses. The council borrowed £285m from the PWLB during the year at an average 4.54%, over half of it to refinance old debt that had been costing 5.51%, and net external borrowing rose £136.3m, adding £4.75m a year to the interest bill. Almost all the new loans are one-to-three-year money: £268m (17% of the £1,596m debt pile) now falls due within twelve months, so Croydon returns to the market constantly. All statutory borrowing limits were complied with. EFS / distress

Middlesbrough

UA · England · E06000002 · 34 documents (1 read)
Borrowing 170% of NRE (FY2024/25) rank vs peers →

Middlesbrough's draft (pre-audit) accounts show a council improving but still thin: usable reserves fell 9% to £92.0m, cash and treasury investments dropped sharply (investments held £21.3m → £8.8m) under children's-social-care and special-educational-needs spending pressure, and a large slug of PWLB debt matured into short-term borrowing, pushing current liabilities up £21.2m. The genuinely good news is that of the £13.4m exceptional financial support approved for 2024/25, only £2.4m was needed and none of it was borrowed. Borrowing need (CFR) edged up £7.8m to £307.9m against £4.8m of MRP repayment. watch items

Bridgend

WPA · Wales · W06000013 · 51 documents (1 read)
MHCLG: England only rank vs peers →

A healthy small Welsh unitary: external borrowing fell to £99.7m (from £103.8m) at an average 4.63%, investments rose to £44.5m earning 4.73%, and the council repaid £3.7m of debt while taking just £5m of new 16-month PWLB money to cover maturities. The one item worth a diary note: £19.25m of LOBO loans — old loans the lender can demand back at set dates — are nominally due in 2054, but the report itself says they are likely to be called earlier, with the next call window on 22 July 2026. Full compliance with the treasury codes is reported. watch items
